displayQuote: Wonder is the beginning of wisdom

meta.title: Who really said "Wonder is the beginning of wisdom"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Socrates is credited with “Wonder is the beginning of wisdom” — but Plato’s Theaetetus actually says “philosophy,” not “wisdom.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Wonder is the beginning of wisdom'?
meta.ogDescription: The line traces to Plato’s Socrates (Theaetetus 155d) — but the real text reads “wonder is the only beginning of philosophy.” “Wisdom” is a paraphrase.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: c. 470–399 BCE · Athenian philosopher, as voiced in Plato’s Theaetetus (c. 369 BCE)
answer.sourceLine: Widely and reasonably credited to Socrates: the thought is genuinely his as recorded in Plato’s Theaetetus 155d ↗, where Socrates tells Theaetetus that “wonder is the only beginning of philosophy.” But no primary source pins this exact wording — Socrates wrote nothing himself, and the surviving text says “philosophy,” not “wisdom.” The popular line is a later paraphrase.

source.heading: Where it really comes from
source.excerpt: Theodorus seems to be a pretty good guesser about your nature. For this feeling of wonder shows that you are a philosopher, since wonder is the only beginning of philosophy, and he who said that Iris was the child of Thaumas made a good genealogy.
trail: Plato’s Socrates: “wonder is the only beginning of philosophy” — Theaetetus 155d, trans. Fowler ↗.
Aristotle echoes the same idea a generation later: “it is through wonder that men now begin and originally began to philosophize” — Metaphysics 982b ↗.
The “wisdom” wording circulates today as a verbatim Socrates quote — e.g. on Goodreads ↗ — with no ancient source for that exact phrasing.
source.excerptNote: The popular one-liner “Wonder is the beginning of wisdom” compresses and reworks this passage. The swap is defensible — philosophia literally means ‘love of wisdom’ — but it is a paraphrase, not a translation of what Plato wrote.
source.rightsNote: The underlying text is ancient and long in the public domain; Fowler’s 1921 translation is also public domain in the U.S. The tidy modern wording “Wonder is the beginning of wisdom” is an anonymous paraphrase with no identifiable author.

author.name: Socrates
author.heading: Socrates
author.bio: Socrates was an Athenian philosopher and the founding figure of Western moral philosophy. Famously, he wrote nothing — everything we have of him comes secondhand, chiefly through the dialogues of his student Plato and the writings of Xenophon. The saying about wonder is put in his mouth by Plato in the Theaetetus, a dialogue on the nature of knowledge, where wonder (Greek thauma) is named as the root from which philosophy grows.

copyAttribution: Wonder is the beginning of wisdom — attributed to Socrates. It's a paraphrase of Plato's Theaetetus (155d), where the actual text reads "wonder is the only beginning of philosophy."

misattribution.heading: How it gets mis-cited
misattribution.intro: This one isn’t attached to the wrong person so much as attached to the wrong words. The sentiment is authentically Socratic, but it is routinely quoted as if it were a verbatim line from Socrates himself.

items.scope: Presented as a verbatim quote from
items.why: Socrates left no writings; the words are Plato’s, and the surviving text (Theaetetus 155d ↗) reads “wonder is the only beginning of philosophy,” not “wisdom.”
Aristotle does tie wonder to the origins of inquiry (Metaphysics 982b ↗: “through wonder that men…began to philosophize”), but his phrasing is not this line either.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is genuinely Socratic by way of Plato’s Theaetetus ↗; the word “wisdom” is a modern paraphrase of “philosophy” — which, literally, already means ‘love of wisdom.’

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In the Theaetetus, Socrates and the gifted young mathematician Theaetetus are trying to define knowledge itself. When Theaetetus confesses that puzzling over these questions makes his head spin, Socrates reassures him: that dizzy feeling of wonder (Greek thaumazein) is not a weakness but the very mark of a philosopher.

Socrates seals the point with a pun on myth: the rainbow-goddess Iris, messenger between gods and mortals, was said to be the daughter of Thaumas — ‘Wonder.’ Philosophy, he suggests, is likewise born of wonder. Aristotle took up the same claim in the Metaphysics, and it echoes down through Descartes, Whitehead and beyond as a founding motto of Western thought.
detailsBody: The paraphrase survives because it is essentially faithful: philosophia is a compound of philo- (loving) and sophia (wisdom). To say philosophy begins in wonder is, near enough, to say the pursuit of wisdom begins in wonder. The quote crosses from ‘accurate’ to ‘paraphrase’ only when it is presented inside quotation marks as Socrates’s own words.
